guides.title: Periodic Trends: Atomic Radius, Ionization Energy and Electronegativity
guides.summary: How and why atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity change across periods and down groups of the periodic table, with the effective nuclear charge model, the famous exceptions, and worked comparisons.

sections.heading: Why the Periodic Table Predicts Behavior: Periods, Groups and Electron Configuration
sections.body:
The periodic table is not a filing cabinet of facts; it is a prediction machine. Arrange the elements in order of increasing atomic number — the count of protons in the nucleus — and chemical and physical properties repeat in regular cycles. Dmitri Mendeleev exploited this periodicity in 1869, famously leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and predicting the properties of gallium and germanium years before anyone isolated them; his predicted density for the element he called eka-silicon, about 5.5 grams per cubic centimeter, matched germanium's measured 5.32 remarkably well. The modern explanation for why periodicity exists came half a century later from quantum mechanics: the properties of an element are governed almost entirely by the arrangement of its electrons, and electron arrangements themselves repeat in cycles as shells fill.

Electrons occupy orbitals grouped into shells labeled by the principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3 and so on, and within shells into subshells labeled s, p, d and f, holding a maximum of 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons respectively. A row of the periodic table — a period — corresponds to the filling of a new principal shell. Period 2 runs from lithium to neon as the n = 2 shell fills with up to eight electrons; period 3 runs sodium to argon as n = 3 fills its s and p subshells. A column — a group — collects elements whose outermost shells hold the same number of electrons in the same kinds of orbitals. Every alkali metal in group 1 has a single s electron beyond a noble-gas core: lithium is [He]2s¹, sodium is [Ne]3s¹, potassium is [Ar]4s¹. Every halogen in group 17 sits one electron short of a filled shell. Because chemistry is conducted almost exclusively by these outermost, or valence, electrons, elements in a group behave as a family.

The three properties this guide develops — atomic radius, ionization energy and electronegativity — are the quantitative expression of that family behavior. Atomic radius measures how large the electron cloud is. Ionization energy measures how tightly the atom holds its outermost electron. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom bonded to another pulls shared electrons toward itself. These are not independent facts to memorize separately: all three are controlled by the same underlying tug-of-war between the positively charged nucleus and the negatively charged electrons, moderated by how much inner electrons screen the outer ones. Learn the engine, described in the next section as effective nuclear charge, and the trends of all three properties — plus electron affinity, metallic character and reactivity — follow from a single line of reasoning rather than from a stack of flashcards.

A note on reading the table's geography will help throughout. Across a period means moving left to right, from metals through metalloids to nonmetals, ending at a noble gas. Down a group means moving top to bottom, adding a whole new electron shell at each step. The two directions have opposite effects on most properties, which produces the diagonal character of the table: the smallest, most electron-greedy atoms cluster at the top right around fluorine, and the largest, most electron-releasing atoms sit at the bottom left around cesium and francium. Nearly every periodic trend question reduces to locating the elements involved on this diagonal map.

sections.heading: Effective Nuclear Charge and Shielding: The Engine Behind Every Trend
sections.body:
Every periodic trend in this guide is driven by one physical quantity: the effective nuclear charge, written Z_eff, which is the net positive charge an outer electron actually experiences. The nucleus of a chlorine atom carries 17 protons, but a valence electron in chlorine does not feel the full pull of all 17, because ten inner-shell electrons sit between it and the nucleus, repelling it and partially canceling the nuclear attraction. This canceling is called shielding or screening. A useful first approximation is Z_eff = Z minus S, where Z is the atomic number and S is the number of shielding inner-core electrons. For chlorine that gives roughly 17 − 10 = 7; for sodium, 11 − 10 = 1. More refined estimates, such as those from Slater's rules published in 1930 or from quantum-mechanical calculations by Clementi and Raimondi in 1963, give non-integer values — about 6.1 for a chlorine valence electron and 2.5 for sodium's — but the simple core-counting version captures the trend logic perfectly well.

The crucial insight is how Z_eff changes as you move around the table. Across a period, each successive element adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same outer shell. Electrons in the same shell shield one another poorly, because they are at roughly the same average distance from the nucleus rather than between each other and the nucleus. So the added proton's pull is felt almost fully: Z_eff climbs steadily across a period, from about +1 at sodium to about +7 at chlorine. The valence electrons of the later elements are gripped by a much stronger net charge, and everything follows from that grip — the cloud contracts, electrons become harder to remove, and the atom pulls harder on bonding electrons.

Down a group, the story is different. Each step adds a full new shell: sodium's valence electron lives in n = 3, potassium's in n = 4, cesium's in n = 6. The proton count grows enormously — cesium has 55 protons to sodium's 11 — but the added inner electrons are effective shielders, and the core charge felt by the lone outer electron stays roughly constant at about +1 for every alkali metal. What changes down a group is not the net charge but the distance: the valence electron occupies an orbital with a larger principal quantum number, farther on average from the nucleus, and Coulomb's law makes attraction fall off with distance. Farther means bigger radius, weaker hold, easier removal.

Two refinements complete the engine. First, penetration: within a shell, s electrons spend more time close to the nucleus than p electrons, which penetrate more than d, which penetrate more than f. Penetrating electrons feel a higher Z_eff and are held more tightly, which is why subshell energies order as s < p < d < f within a shell, and why several famous exceptions in ionization energy arise. Second, poor shielding by d and f electrons: because d and f orbitals are diffuse and poor at screening, elements that follow the filling of a d or f block feel unusually high effective charge. This causes the d-block contraction, which makes gallium essentially the same size as aluminum above it, and the lanthanide contraction, which makes hafnium almost identical in radius to zirconium and explains why the heavy transition metals such as platinum and gold are so dense and so noble. Keep Z_eff, distance, penetration and shielding in view, and every trend that follows is a corollary rather than a new fact.

sections.heading: Atomic Radius and Atomic Radii: What the Size of an Atom Means and How It Is Measured
sections.body:
An atom has no hard edge. Its electron cloud is a probability distribution that fades smoothly to zero, so the radius of an atom cannot be measured the way you would measure a marble; it must be defined operationally, and different definitions give somewhat different numbers. The most common is the covalent radius: half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond. The bond length of the Cl–Cl bond in a chlorine molecule is measured, by electron diffraction or spectroscopy, at about 198 picometers, so the covalent radius of chlorine is taken as roughly 99 picometers. A picometer is one trillionth of a meter; atomic radii run from about 31 pm for helium to around 265 pm for cesium, which is a factor of nearly nine between the smallest and largest neutral atoms.

For metals, which do not form discrete diatomic molecules, the metallic radius serves instead: half the distance between adjacent nuclei in the solid metal's crystal lattice, obtained from X-ray crystallography. Sodium's metallic radius is about 186 pm, copper's about 128 pm. For atoms that do not readily bond at all — the noble gases — and for gauging how close non-bonded atoms can approach, chemists use the van der Waals radius, half the distance between nuclei of adjacent, non-bonded atoms in a crystal. Van der Waals radii are systematically larger than covalent radii for the same element: carbon's covalent radius is about 76 pm, while its van der Waals radius is about 170 pm. This is why published tables of atomic radius disagree with one another; they may be reporting different kinds of radius, or covalent radii derived from different sets of compounds. The trends, however, are identical whichever definition is used consistently.

Why does size matter chemically? Radius controls or strongly influences an enormous range of behavior. Bond lengths are approximately sums of covalent radii, so radii let you estimate the geometry of molecules never yet made. Lattice energies of ionic solids scale inversely with the distance between ion centers, so smaller ions make harder, higher-melting salts — magnesium oxide, built from small Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, melts at 2,852 °C, whereas sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. The charge density of an ion, its charge divided by its size, governs how strongly it polarizes neighbors and organizes water molecules around itself, which shapes solubility and biology alike; the reason lithium behaves oddly among alkali metals traces largely to its tiny radius. Catalysis, alloy formation, and which elements can substitute for one another in minerals all hinge on comparative size.

It is also worth internalizing what an atom mostly is: empty space, in the classical picture. The nucleus, containing better than 99.9 percent of the mass, has a radius on the order of a few femtometers — a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom. If an atom were scaled to a sports stadium, the nucleus would be roughly the size of a pea at the center, with the electron cloud filling the stands. The radius we discuss in this guide is the size of that cloud, and the trends in the next section describe how the tug-of-war between nuclear charge and shell distance stretches or compresses it across the table.

sections.heading: Atomic Radius Across a Period and Down a Group: The Trend and the Reasons
sections.body:
The two master trends in atomic radius are stated in one sentence each. Across a period, from left to right, atomic radius decreases. Down a group, from top to bottom, atomic radius increases. Both follow directly from the effective nuclear charge engine, and both are worth walking through with real numbers.

Take period 3. Sodium's covalent radius is about 166 pm; magnesium's about 141; aluminum 121; silicon 111; phosphorus 107; sulfur 105; chlorine 102; argon, by the definitions that apply to it, around 106 (noble-gas values are measured differently, which is why argon appears slightly out of line in some tables). The overall contraction from sodium to chlorine is nearly 40 percent. The cause is the poor mutual shielding of same-shell electrons: each step right adds a proton that is felt almost fully by every valence electron, so Z_eff climbs from roughly +1 to +7 across the row, and the same n = 3 shell is pulled inward ever more tightly. Nothing about the shell's principal quantum number changes; the electrons simply orbit, on average, closer to an increasingly powerful nucleus. The same pattern repeats in every period: lithium at about 128 pm shrinks to fluorine at about 64 pm across period 2.

Now go down group 1. Lithium is about 128 pm, sodium 166, potassium 203, rubidium 220, cesium 244, and francium, from relativistic calculations since it is too radioactive for conventional measurement, roughly comparable to cesium or slightly smaller. Each step down adds an entire new principal shell — the outermost electron moves from n = 2 in lithium to n = 6 in cesium — and each new core of inner electrons shields the added protons almost completely, holding Z_eff near +1 for the whole family. Distance wins, and the atoms swell. The competition between these two factors is not close in practice: adding a shell outweighs the accompanying increase in nuclear charge every time, which is why the size ordering down any main group is monotonic.

Combining the two trends gives the diagonal rule of thumb: atoms grow toward the bottom left of the table and shrink toward the top right. Helium is the smallest atom; francium and cesium are the largest. When asked to rank atoms by size, place them on the table and reason geographically, taking care with diagonal comparisons where the two trends conflict — comparing, say, phosphorus and bromine requires more thought than a same-row or same-column pair, and honest answers sometimes require data.

The transition metals complicate the middle of the long periods in an instructive way. Crossing the 3d series from scandium to zinc, radii shrink at first, flatten, and even rise slightly at the end, because the electrons being added enter the inner 3d subshell, where they shield the outer 4s electrons moderately well; the contraction is therefore gentler than in the main groups. Two consequences of d and f filling deserve their own mention. Gallium, immediately after the first d series, has a covalent radius of about 122 pm, essentially identical to aluminum's 121 above it — the d-block contraction. And the lanthanide contraction, caused by the poorly shielding 4f electrons filling from cerium to lutetium, shrinks the third transition series so much that hafnium (159 pm) is virtually the same size as zirconium (160 pm) despite having 32 more electrons. That size coincidence makes hafnium and zirconium notoriously difficult to separate chemically, and it underlies the high densities of osmium and iridium, the densest elements known at about 22.6 grams per cubic centimeter.

sections.heading: Ionic Radius: Cations, Anions and Isoelectronic Series
sections.body:
Atoms change size dramatically when they become ions, and the direction of change is easy to reason out. Removing electrons makes an ion smaller; adding electrons makes it larger. A cation is smaller than its parent atom for two stacked reasons. First, the electrons removed are usually the entire outer shell: sodium at [Ne]3s¹ loses its lone n = 3 electron to become Na⁺ with the compact [Ne] configuration, so the ion's outermost electrons live a full shell closer to the nucleus. Second, the remaining electrons are now fewer while the proton count is unchanged, so each remaining electron feels less electron–electron repulsion and a higher effective nuclear charge, tightening the cloud further. The numbers are striking: sodium's metallic radius of about 186 pm collapses to about 102 pm for Na⁺, and magnesium's 160 pm falls to 72 pm for Mg²⁺. The higher the positive charge, the more severe the contraction — Al³⁺ is only about 54 pm.

An anion is larger than its parent atom for the mirror-image reason. Chlorine gains an electron to become Cl⁻: the proton count stays at 17, but 18 electrons now share the same nuclear attraction, so each is held less tightly, and the added electron–electron repulsion puffs the cloud outward. Chlorine's covalent radius of about 99 pm balloons to roughly 181 pm for chloride. Oxygen at about 66 pm becomes O²⁻ at about 140 pm. As a rule, common anions are large — 130 to 220 pm — while common cations are small — 50 to 170 pm — which is why, in most ionic crystals such as sodium chloride, the picture to hold in mind is big anions packed together with small cations tucked into the gaps between them.

The cleanest demonstration that nuclear charge controls size comes from an isoelectronic series: a set of ions and atoms that all have exactly the same number of electrons. Consider the ten-electron series, all with the neon configuration: O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺. Their radii run approximately 140, 133, 69 (a non-bonded measure), 102, 72 and 54 pm respectively — but compare only the ions and the ordering is strict: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺. Every member has ten electrons in identical configuration; the only variable is the number of protons pulling on them, rising from 8 to 13 across the series. More protons, same electrons, smaller ion. If an exam question asks you to rank an isoelectronic set, count protons and you are done: highest atomic number is smallest.

Ionic size has heavyweight consequences. Lattice energy — the energy released when gaseous ions assemble into a crystal — grows as ions shrink and charges rise, following Coulomb's law; this is why MgO is refractory enough to line furnaces while NaCl dissolves in your soup. Solubility patterns, the selectivity of biological ion channels that admit K⁺ but exclude the smaller Na⁺ on the basis of hydration and fit, the substitution of ions in minerals, and the polarizing power of small, highly charged cations, which drags ionic bonds toward covalency as described by Fajans' rules, all trace back to ionic radii. One caution for data readers: tabulated ionic radii, most famously the Shannon radii published in 1976, depend on the ion's coordination number — Na⁺ is listed at 99 pm in four-coordination and 102 pm in six — so small discrepancies between sources are normal and not errors.

sections.heading: Ionization Energy: Definition, Units and the First Ionization Energy Trend
sections.body:
Ionization energy is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from a neutral atom in the gas phase, producing a cation and a free electron: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. The gas-phase specification matters, because it isolates the atom from lattice and solvent effects and makes values comparable across the table. The quantity is always positive — removing an electron from any atom costs energy, since the electron is bound — and it is usually quoted in kilojoules per mole of atoms or in electronvolts per atom, where 1 eV per atom equals 96.485 kJ/mol. The first ionization energy of hydrogen is 1,312 kJ/mol, or 13.6 eV, a number that falls straight out of the Bohr model and quantum mechanics alike.

The periodic trend mirrors atomic radius inverted, because the same engine drives both. Across a period, ionization energy generally increases: Z_eff climbs, the valence electrons sit closer to a stronger net charge, and prying one loose costs more. Down a group, ionization energy decreases: the outermost electron occupies a shell ever farther from the nucleus behind ever more shielding, so it is held loosely and departs cheaply. The extremes are exactly where the radius map predicts. Helium has the highest first ionization energy of any element at 2,372 kJ/mol; neon follows at 2,081; fluorine at 1,681. At the other corner, cesium sits at 376 kJ/mol and francium at about 393 — slightly above cesium, an anomaly explained by relativistic contraction of francium's 7s orbital, one of the rare places heavy-element physics visibly bends a trend.

Walking across period 2 with real values shows both the trend and its texture: lithium 520, beryllium 899, boron 801, carbon 1,086, nitrogen 1,402, oxygen 1,314, fluorine 1,681, neon 2,081 kJ/mol. The climb is unmistakable — neon costs four times lithium — but notice the two stumbles, from beryllium to boron and from nitrogen to oxygen, where the value drops instead of rising. These are not measurement noise; they are fingerprints of subshell structure, and the next section dissects them. Period 3 repeats the pattern one energy floor down: sodium 496, magnesium 738, aluminum 578, silicon 786, phosphorus 1,012, sulfur 1,000, chlorine 1,251, argon 1,521 kJ/mol.

Ionization energy is the most direct experimental window into electronic structure, and it connects to chemistry everywhere. Elements with low first ionization energies are metals and reducing agents: the alkali metals ionize so cheaply that they exist in nature only as +1 cations, and the trend down the group — lithium 520, sodium 496, potassium 419, rubidium 403, cesium 376 — tracks their escalating violence in water. Elements with very high ionization energies cling to their electrons and either share them covalently, like carbon and nitrogen, or refuse most chemistry altogether, like helium and neon. Photoionization underlies the photoelectric effect, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and the ionosphere itself, where solar ultraviolet strips electrons from atmospheric atoms. When you see a first ionization energy, read it as a price tag: how much does the universe charge to turn this atom into a cation? The periodic table's answer ranges over a factor of six, from cesium's bargain 376 to helium's prohibitive 2,372 kJ/mol, and the geography of that pricing is the geography of metallic character itself.

sections.heading: The Famous Exceptions: Why Boron Undercuts Beryllium and Oxygen Undercuts Nitrogen
sections.body:
The saw-toothed exceptions in the first ionization energy trend are among the most instructive details in introductory chemistry, because they cannot be explained by the smooth Z_eff story alone; they force you to look at subshells and at electron pairing. There are two recurring dips in every s–p period, and each has its own mechanism.

The first dip comes between groups 2 and 13: beryllium's ionization energy is 899 kJ/mol, but boron's — despite boron having one more proton — is only 801. The explanation is subshell penetration. Beryllium's outermost electron comes from the filled 2s subshell, and s electrons penetrate close to the nucleus, feel a high effective charge, and sit low in energy. Boron's configuration is [He]2s²2p¹: its most loosely held electron is the lone 2p electron, and p orbitals penetrate less, are shielded partly by the 2s pair beneath them, and sit measurably higher in energy. Removing boron's 2p electron is therefore cheaper than removing one of beryllium's tightly held 2s pair, and the trend dips. Period 3 repeats the effect precisely: magnesium 738, aluminum 578, because aluminum's departing electron is its solitary 3p.

The second dip comes between groups 15 and 16: nitrogen costs 1,402 kJ/mol but oxygen only 1,314. Here the mechanism is electron pairing and exchange energy. Nitrogen's 2p subshell holds three electrons, one in each of the three p orbitals, all spins parallel, exactly as Hund's rule prescribes; this half-filled arrangement is unusually stable, partly because electrons in separate orbitals avoid one another and partly because parallel spins gain quantum-mechanical exchange stabilization. Oxygen's fourth p electron has no empty p orbital left and must pair up in an already occupied one. The two paired electrons share a small region of space and repel each other strongly, so the newest electron is easier to remove than nitrogen's symmetric arrangement would suggest — easier, even, than the bare proton count implies. Sulfur echoes phosphorus the same way in period 3: phosphorus 1,012, sulfur 1,000.

These two exceptions generalize into a principle worth carrying: filled and half-filled subshells are pockets of extra stability, and ionization energies jump when removal would break into one and sag when removal relieves a fresh pairing. The principle also illuminates other corners of the table. It contributes to chromium's configuration of [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ rather than 3d⁴4s², and copper's [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ rather than 3d⁹4s² — the atom promotes an s electron to complete a half-filled or filled d subshell. It helps explain why the noble gases, with completely filled shells, top every period's ionization chart, and why nitrogen's chemistry features a stubbornly strong triple bond and reluctance toward some reactions that oxygen embraces.

A caution for exams and for honest reasoning: the exceptions are local, involving adjacent elements, and they never overturn the large-scale trend. Fluorine still towers over every earlier element in its row; the dips are ripples of 50 to 100 kJ/mol on a rise of 1,500. When ranking ionization energies, apply the general trend first, then check whether any pair of neighbors straddles a group 2–13 or group 15–16 boundary and adjust just that pair. And remember which quantity you are ranking; the exceptions appear in first ionization energies of neutral atoms, not automatically in radii or electronegativities, which follow their own smoother courses through the same territory.

sections.heading: Successive Ionization Energies: How Second and Third Ionizations Reveal Shell Structure
sections.body:
Removing one electron from an atom is only the beginning; every atom with multiple electrons has a ladder of successive ionization energies — the second ionization energy for X⁺(g) → X²⁺(g) + e⁻, the third for the next removal, and so on. Two facts govern the ladder. First, each successive ionization always costs more than the last, because each electron is being pulled away from an increasingly positive ion; with fewer electrons sharing the same nuclear charge, every survivor is bound more tightly. Second, and far more diagnostically, the increase is modest while you are removing electrons from the same valence shell, then suddenly enormous when you break into the noble-gas core beneath. That discontinuity is a direct experimental readout of shell structure — arguably the cleanest evidence for shells that a student ever meets.

The numbers make the point unforgettable. Sodium's first ionization energy is 496 kJ/mol; its second is 4,562 — nearly ten times larger — because the second electron must come out of the compact, neon-like core. Magnesium runs 738, then 1,451, then a wall at 7,733 kJ/mol for the third electron: two affordable valence removals, then the core. Aluminum runs 578, 1,817, 2,745, and then leaps to 11,577 for the fourth. The pattern is a staircase with one giant step, and the position of the giant step counts the valence electrons. Given a mystery element whose successive ionization energies are, say, 590, 1,145, then 4,912 and 6,491, you can say with confidence it has two valence electrons and belongs to group 2 — that particular staircase is calcium's.

This is also the energetic explanation for the charges ions actually adopt. Sodium forms Na⁺ and never Na²⁺ in ordinary chemistry because no chemical process — no lattice energy, no hydration energy — can repay a 4,562 kJ/mol invoice for breaching the core. Magnesium happily forms Mg²⁺ because both removals are valence-shell prices that the enormous lattice energies of its compounds more than refund, but Mg³⁺ is unreachable. Aluminum stops at Al³⁺. The octet rule, often taught as a bookkeeping mnemonic, is at bottom this wall in the ionization ladder: chemistry proceeds until the next electron would come from a closed shell, and there it stops.

Successive ionizations also explain why the maximum common charge climbs across the table's left side and why transition metals are different. Iron's ionizations to Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ both remove electrons from the 4s and then 3d levels without breaching an inert core, which is why iron has two common cations and why transition metals in general display multiple oxidation states — their d electrons sit close in energy to their s electrons, offering several affordable rungs before any wall. The special stability of Fe³⁺, with its half-filled 3d⁵ configuration, is the pairing-energy principle from the previous section reappearing in ionic form.

When you meet successive-ionization data on an exam, the procedure is mechanical: scan the list for the largest ratio between consecutive values; the number of electrons removed before that jump equals the element's group number among the main groups. When you meet it in nature, read it as the reason the ionic world is so orderly — why table salt is NaCl and not NaCl₂, why lime is CaO and not CaO₂'s ionic analogue, and why the charges on the ions of the main-group elements can be predicted from a glance at the periodic table's columns.

sections.heading: Electron Affinity: The Energy of Gaining an Electron, and Why Chlorine Beats Fluorine
sections.body:
Electron affinity is ionization energy's mirror image: the energy change when a neutral gas-phase atom gains an electron, X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). For most nonmetals this process releases energy — the incoming electron falls into the attraction of a nucleus whose pull is not fully screened — and by the most common bookkeeping the release is written as a negative enthalpy change: chlorine's electron affinity is −349 kJ/mol, meaning 349 kJ are given off per mole of electrons captured. Beware sign conventions when reading tables: some sources report electron affinities as positive numbers meaning energy released, others as signed enthalpy changes; always check which convention a table uses before comparing values. Either way, the chemical meaning is the same — a large release means the atom strongly wants the extra electron.

The periodic pattern is looser than the radius and ionization trends, but its outline follows the same engine. Electron affinity generally becomes more exothermic across a period, as rising Z_eff makes the atom a deeper well for an incoming electron, and it is most exothermic among the halogens, each one electron short of a closed shell: fluorine −328, chlorine −349, bromine −325, iodine −295 kJ/mol. The noble gases, with no vacancy in their valence shells, do not bind an extra electron at all — their electron affinities are positive or effectively zero, since the newcomer would have to open a whole new shell. Groups 2 and 15 show characteristically weak affinities for reasons the ionization exceptions already taught: beryllium and magnesium would have to place the new electron in a higher p subshell, and nitrogen would have to disturb its stable half-filled p³ set by pairing, so nitrogen's electron affinity is approximately zero.

The most celebrated anomaly is that chlorine, not fluorine, has the most exothermic electron affinity of any element. On raw trend logic fluorine should win: it is smaller, its Z_eff on the valence shell is high, and its anion is closer to the nucleus. But fluorine's compact n = 2 valence shell is so crowded that the incoming electron suffers intense repulsion from the electrons already packed into that tiny volume, and the repulsion taxes away part of the attraction's payoff. Chlorine's roomier n = 3 shell accepts the guest with less protest. The same second-row congestion effect makes oxygen's affinity (−141 kJ/mol) weaker than sulfur's (−200), a paired anomaly worth remembering because examiners love it. Do not over-extend the lesson, though: fluorine remains the more reactive halogen overall, because reactivity is set by full reaction energetics — including F₂'s unusually weak bond and fluoride's enormous lattice and hydration energies — not by electron affinity alone.

A further subtlety matters for ionic compounds: second electron affinities are always endothermic. Adding an electron to an already negative ion means forcing like charges together; O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) costs about +744 kJ/mol. The familiar oxide ion exists in crystals only because lattice energy repays the debt with interest — isolated O²⁻ in the gas phase is not stable at all, a fact that surprises students and appears regularly in Born–Haber cycle problems. Electron affinity's practical significance runs through all of that territory: it is a term in every Born–Haber analysis of ionic solids, a component of the Mulliken definition of electronegativity described in the next section, and the property that makes halogens the table's great electron scavengers and oxidizing agents.

sections.heading: Electronegativity: Pauling's Scale, Other Scales, and What the Numbers Mean
sections.body:
Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a chemical bond to attract the shared bonding electrons toward itself. The italicized phrase is the crucial distinction from the last two sections: ionization energy and electron affinity are properties of isolated gas-phase atoms and are measured in energy units, whereas electronegativity describes an atom's behavior inside a bond and is a derived, dimensionless index rather than a directly measurable quantity. That is why several scales exist, each anchoring the concept in a different measurement — yet all agreeing on the ordering that matters for chemistry.

The canonical scale is Linus Pauling's, introduced in 1932. Pauling noticed that a bond between two different atoms, A–B, is almost always stronger than the average of the A–A and B–B bonds, and he attributed the extra strength to ionic character: partial charge separation adds electrostatic attraction on top of covalent sharing. He converted that excess bond energy into a number for each element, fixing the scale so fluorine — the most electronegative element — sits at 3.98, usually quoted as 4.0. Key values every chemist eventually knows by heart: oxygen 3.44, chlorine 3.16, nitrogen 3.04, bromine 2.96, sulfur and carbon 2.58 and 2.55, hydrogen 2.20, phosphorus 2.19, silicon 1.90, aluminum 1.61, magnesium 1.31, sodium 0.93, potassium 0.82, cesium 0.79. Francium is often listed at 0.7, though relativistic calculations suggest cesium is actually the least electronegative real element — a nuance, not a trend-breaker.

Other scales triangulate the same idea. Robert Mulliken proposed in 1934 that electronegativity is simply the average of ionization energy and electron affinity: an atom that both resists losing electrons and rewards gaining them will hoard bonding density. Mulliken values correlate almost linearly with Pauling's, which is reassuring — two independent definitions land on the same chemistry. The Allred–Rochow scale (1958) defines electronegativity as the electrostatic force the effective nuclear charge exerts at the covalent radius, tying the concept explicitly to the Z_eff engine of this guide, and the Allen scale (1989) uses the average energy of the valence electrons from spectroscopy. Tables you meet will nearly always be Pauling unless labeled otherwise.

What do the numbers buy you? Difference in electronegativity between bonded atoms, ΔEN, is the standard quick estimate of bond polarity. Identical atoms share evenly; a modest difference produces a polar covalent bond with partial charges, written δ+ and δ−; a large difference produces essentially ionic bonding. The conventional though admittedly fuzzy cutoffs are: ΔEN below about 0.4, treat as nonpolar covalent; between roughly 0.4 and 1.7 to 2.0, polar covalent; above that, predominantly ionic. Thus H–H (0.0) is nonpolar, C–H (0.35) is nearly so — the quiet fact underlying the low polarity of hydrocarbons — O–H (1.24) is strongly polar, and Na–Cl (2.23) is ionic. Electronegativity also assigns oxidation states, since the convention hands both bonding electrons to the more electronegative partner; it predicts the direction of dipole moments; it explains why hydrogen bonding requires H attached to N, O or F, the three small atoms electronegative enough to strip hydrogen's electron density; and it rationalizes reaction chemistry from the acidity of O–H versus C–H bonds to the polarity-driven mechanisms of organic chemistry. Wherever a chemist asks who holds the electrons in this bond, electronegativity is the first answer consulted.

sections.heading: Electronegativity Trends Across the Table and Bond Character: Ionic, Polar Covalent, Covalent
sections.body:
Electronegativity follows the now-familiar diagonal geography, and by this point in the guide the reasons can be stated in a breath. Across a period it increases: effective nuclear charge rises, the atom is smaller, and bonding electrons shared with it sit close to a strong, poorly screened nucleus. Down a group it decreases: the valence region lies farther from the nucleus behind thicker shielding, so the atom's grip on shared density weakens. The most electronegative elements therefore crowd the top right — fluorine 3.98, oxygen 3.44, nitrogen 3.04 and chlorine 3.16 form the aggressive quartet — while the least electronegative crowd the bottom left, with cesium at 0.79. Noble gases are usually left unassigned on the Pauling scale because they form so few bonds, though values are computed on other scales, and the heavier ones do have chemistry: xenon bonds with fluorine and oxygen precisely because those are the only partners electronegative enough to pry at its tightly held electrons, as in XeF₂ and XeF₄, known since 1962.

The workhorse application is classifying bonds. Compute ΔEN and locate it on the continuum. Cl–Cl at 0.0 is purely covalent. C–H at 0.35 is effectively nonpolar, which is why fats and oils, built from C–H and C–C bonds, are nonpolar solvents and why water refuses to mix with them. C–O at 0.89 and O–H at 1.24 are strongly polar covalent; the O–H bonds of water, bent at 104.5 degrees so their bond dipoles add rather than cancel, give water its large dipole moment, its high boiling point through hydrogen bonding, and its power as a solvent for ionic substances. N–H at 0.84 makes ammonia polar and underlies the hydrogen bonding that stitches together DNA base pairs and protein backbones. Na–Cl at 2.23 and Cs–F at 3.19 — the largest ΔEN available between stable elements — sit firmly in ionic territory, existing as lattices of discrete ions rather than as molecules.

Treat the cutoffs honestly, though: bond character is a continuum, not three boxes. Hydrogen fluoride's ΔEN of 1.78 would label it ionic by some textbook thresholds, yet HF is a discrete covalent molecule, merely a very polar one; conversely, silver chloride behaves less ionically than its ΔEN suggests because the large, squishy chloride ion is polarized by the cation. Fajans' rules capture the corrections: small, highly charged cations and large, easily deformed anions push nominally ionic compounds toward covalent character, which is why AlCl₃ sublimes as a covalent dimer while NaCl sits at the ionic pole. Percent ionic character can also be estimated from measured dipole moments — HF comes out near 41 percent ionic — reminding us that the ΔEN estimate is a first pass, not a verdict.

Two more consequences round out the picture. Electronegativity equalizes across molecules: in carbon dioxide each C=O bond is polar, but the linear geometry cancels the two bond dipoles, so the molecule as a whole is nonpolar — bond polarity and molecular polarity are different questions, joined by geometry. And electronegativity anchors the metal–nonmetal divide itself: elements below about 1.9 on the Pauling scale are broadly metallic in behavior, those above about 2.2 are nonmetals, and the metalloids — boron 2.04, silicon 1.90, germanium 2.01, arsenic 2.18, antimony 2.05, tellurium 2.1 — occupy the ambiguous staircase between, their intermediate electron-holding power the very thing that makes silicon and germanium semiconductors rather than conductors or insulators.

sections.heading: Metallic Character, Reactivity and the Chemistry the Trends Predict
sections.body:
Metallic character is not a separate trend so much as the human-scale summary of the three quantitative ones. A metal, chemically speaking, is an element that loses electrons easily: low ionization energy, low electronegativity, large radius. A nonmetal is an element that gains or hoards electrons: high ionization energy, exothermic electron affinity, high electronegativity, small radius. It follows without further argument that metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period — the exact inverse of the electronegativity map — and that the most metallic elements are cesium and francium at the bottom left while the most nonmetallic is fluorine at the top right. The staircase of metalloids from boron to tellurium marks the frontier where the two behaviors trade dominance, and even within single groups you can watch the handover: in group 14, carbon is a nonmetal, silicon and germanium are semiconducting metalloids, tin is a metal with a nonmetallic allotrope, and lead is unambiguously metallic. Group 15 runs from gaseous nonmetallic nitrogen to metallic bismuth the same way.

Reactivity follows, but in opposite directions for the two families, which is a favorite exam distinction. For metals, reactivity increases down a group: the operative step in metallic chemistry is losing electrons, and that gets cheaper as ionization energy falls. Lithium fizzes politely in water; sodium darts and may ignite; potassium bursts into lilac flame on contact; rubidium and cesium react violently. The alkaline earths echo the pattern a notch gentler — magnesium reacts with steam, calcium with cold water. For nonmetals, reactivity increases up a group: the operative step is gaining electrons, and the pull is strongest where electronegativity and effective nuclear charge peak. Fluorine is the most ferociously reactive element known, combining with nearly everything including glass and xenon; chlorine is a strong oxidizer; bromine and iodine are progressively milder. The halogen displacement series demonstrates the ordering in a test tube: bubble chlorine through a solution of bromide or iodide and the free halogen appears, because chlorine out-pulls both for electrons, while iodine can displace neither.

The trends also organize compound behavior. Oxides progress from basic to acidic across a period: sodium oxide dissolves to give strongly alkaline solutions, magnesium oxide is basic, aluminum oxide is amphoteric — reacting with both acids and bases — silicon dioxide is weakly acidic, and the oxides of phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine dissolve to give outright acids, which is the chemistry behind sulfuric and phosphoric acid manufacture and behind acid rain. Hydrides run a similar course from ionic, hydride-ion salts like NaH on the left to covalent, acidic HCl on the right. Bond types between elements can be anticipated the same way: metal plus nonmetal from opposite corners yields ionic solids; two nonmetals yield covalent molecules; metals with each other yield alloys and metallic bonding.

One last organizing idea deserves mention: the diagonal relationship. Elements diagonally adjacent in periods 2 and 3 — lithium and magnesium, beryllium and aluminum, boron and silicon — resemble each other because moving one step right (smaller, more electronegative) and one step down (larger, less electronegative) roughly cancels, leaving similar charge density. Lithium, alone among alkali metals, forms a nitride and a poorly soluble carbonate, just as magnesium does; beryllium's amphoteric oxide and covalent chloride mimic aluminum's. The diagonal relationship is the trends composing with one another — a reminder that the periodic table's predictive power comes not from any single trend but from their interplay.

sections.heading: Using the Trends Together: Worked Comparisons and Reasoning Templates
sections.body:
Knowing the trends is different from deploying them cleanly under pressure, so this section works through comparisons the way an examiner expects, with the reasoning spelled out. The universal template has three moves: locate the elements on the table; identify whether the comparison is within a period, within a group, or diagonal; then argue from effective nuclear charge and shell number, naming the winner. Never answer with the bare trend — because it is further right — without the mechanism; the mechanism is what the marks are for.

Comparison one: which is larger, sulfur or oxygen? Same group, sulfur one period lower. Sulfur's valence electrons occupy n = 3 while oxygen's occupy n = 2; the extra inner shell in sulfur both adds distance and shields the increased nuclear charge, so sulfur is larger — about 105 pm to oxygen's 66. Comparison two: which has the higher first ionization energy, magnesium or aluminum? Same period, aluminum further right, so the naive trend says aluminum — but this pair straddles the group 2 to group 13 boundary, the first classic exception. Aluminum's outermost electron is a lone 3p electron, higher in energy and better shielded than magnesium's 3s pair, so magnesium wins, 738 to 578 kJ/mol. Comparison three: rank Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and F⁻ by size. All three are isoelectronic with neon at ten electrons, so count protons: fluorine has 9, sodium 11, magnesium 12; fewest protons holds its ten electrons loosest, so F⁻ (133 pm) > Na⁺ (102) > Mg²⁺ (72). Comparison four: which bond is more polar, H–Cl or H–Br? Chlorine's electronegativity is 3.16, bromine's 2.96, hydrogen's 2.20; ΔEN is 0.96 versus 0.76, so H–Cl is the more polar bond, consistent with HCl's larger dipole moment.

Diagonal comparisons demand more honesty. Asked whether chlorine or oxygen is more electronegative, you cannot argue from a single trend, because chlorine is further right-and-down while oxygen is up-and-left; you must know the values — oxygen 3.44 beats chlorine 3.16 — or reason that only fluorine exceeds oxygen. A useful memorized ordering handles nearly every such question: F > O > N ≈ Cl > Br > I ≈ S ≈ C > H > metals. Similarly, for sizes across a diagonal such as phosphorus versus bromine, acknowledge the competition and, where permitted, cite data: their covalent radii are in fact close, near 107 and 114 pm.

Common traps to disarm. Do not confuse electron affinity with electronegativity — one is a gas-phase atomic energy, the other a bonding tendency; chlorine tops the first list, fluorine the second. Do not claim fluorine has the highest ionization energy; helium does, and among period 2 elements neon beats fluorine. Do not forget that anion formation enlarges and cation formation shrinks, so ranking Cl versus Cl⁻ versus Cl⁺ is a one-line answer: Cl⁻ > Cl > Cl⁺. Do not apply the nitrogen–oxygen ionization dip to radii or electronegativities, where no such dip exists. And when a question hands you successive ionization energies, hunt the giant leap and read off the group number before doing anything else.

Finally, keep the engine in the foreground of every written answer: number of shells sets distance; effective nuclear charge sets pull; penetration and pairing supply the fine print. Every trend in this guide — radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic character, reactivity — is that one sentence wearing six different costumes, and the student who writes answers in those terms is reasoning like a chemist rather than reciting like a parrot.

sections.heading: Where the Simple Trends Bend: Transition Metals, Lanthanide Contraction and Relativistic Effects
sections.body:
The clean rules of this guide were built on the main-group elements, and they are genuinely reliable there. But a complete picture requires knowing where and why the rules bend, because the bends are not trivia — they explain gold's color, mercury's liquidity, lead's chemistry and the near-identical twins of the fifth and sixth transition rows.

Across the transition series, trends flatten. From scandium to zinc the added electrons enter the inner 3d subshell rather than the outer 4s, and d electrons shield the outer electrons moderately well, so effective nuclear charge on the valence shell grows slowly. Radii contract modestly at first, plateau through the middle of the row, and swell slightly at the end as d–d repulsion builds; first ionization energies drift upward gently rather than climbing steeply. This is why the transition metals resemble one another so much more than main-group neighbors do — iron, cobalt and nickel are chemical siblings in a way that, say, silicon and phosphorus are not — and why they share family traits of variable oxidation states, colored ions and catalytic activity.

The f block bends the table harder. Between lanthanum and hafnium the fourteen lanthanides intervene, filling the deeply buried 4f subshell, and f electrons are the worst shielders of all. The nuclear charge grows by fourteen with almost no compensating screening, so the whole electron cloud ratchets inward — the lanthanide contraction. Its most famous consequence: hafnium, directly below zirconium, has essentially the same radius (about 159 versus 160 pm), so the pair are nearly inseparable chemically; hafnium hid inside zirconium minerals until 1923, one of the last stable elements discovered. The contraction also makes the third transition row unusually dense and noble — osmium and iridium are the densest elements at about 22.6 g/cm³, and platinum and gold owe part of their unreactive majesty to tightly bound electrons.

At the bottom of the table, Einstein takes over from Mendeleev. In atoms of high nuclear charge, inner electrons move at speeds approaching a substantial fraction of light speed — for gold, with Z = 79, the 1s electrons reach roughly 58 percent of c — and special relativity increases their effective mass, contracting the s orbitals and, indirectly, stabilizing them. Relativistic contraction lowers the energy of gold's 6s orbital enough that the 5d-to-6s absorption falls into the visible blue, so gold reflects yellow; silver's analogous absorption stays in the ultraviolet, so silver looks white. Mercury's contracted, stabilized 6s² pair binds so poorly to neighboring atoms that metallic bonding is anomalously weak, and mercury is liquid at room temperature. The same stabilized s² pair, in the p-block, produces the inert pair effect: thallium prefers +1 rather than +3, lead prefers +2 rather than +4 — the 6s electrons sit out the chemistry. Relativity even bends our headline trends: francium's ionization energy (about 393 kJ/mol) is higher than cesium's 376, and calculations place cesium, not francium, as the most electropositive element in practice.

None of this demotes the simple trends; it fences them. Within the main groups, and for any comparison an introductory course will pose, radius, ionization energy and electronegativity follow the Z_eff engine faithfully. The bends are what the same engine produces when d and f shielding and relativistic speeds are fed into it — a satisfying reminder that the periodic table's exceptions are not failures of the theory but its finer predictions.

guides.title: Lewis Structures and Formal Charge
guides.summary: How to draw Lewis structures for molecules and ions, count valence electrons, apply the octet rule, and use formal charges to pick the best structure. Covers resonance, exceptions to the octet rule, the difference between formal charge and oxidation state, and common mistakes.

sections.heading: What a Lewis Structure Shows and Why Chemists Draw Them
sections.body:
A Lewis structure, also called a Lewis dot structure or electron dot diagram, is a two-dimensional map of a molecule's valence electrons, the outermost electrons that do the work of chemical bonding. Each atom is written as its element symbol. Shared pairs of electrons, the covalent bonds, are drawn either as pairs of dots between two symbols or, more commonly, as short lines, one line per shared pair. Electrons that belong to a single atom and take no part in bonding, the lone pairs, are drawn as pairs of dots parked on that atom. A correct Lewis structure accounts for every valence electron in the molecule: none invented, none lost.

The drawing answers questions that a bare molecular formula cannot. The formula C2H6O tells you the ingredients but not the recipe; a Lewis structure distinguishes ethanol, where the oxygen sits between a carbon and a hydrogen, from dimethyl ether, where the oxygen bridges two carbons. That difference in connectivity is the difference between the alcohol in wine and a gas once used as a refrigerant. Lewis structures also reveal bond order, whether two atoms share one, two, or three electron pairs, which in turn predicts relative bond lengths and strengths. They show where lone pairs sit, which controls molecular shape through electron repulsion, and where electric charge accumulates, which controls reactivity. Nearly every mechanism drawn in organic chemistry, every curved arrow showing electrons moving during a reaction, is drawn on top of Lewis structures.

It is worth being clear about what the diagram does not claim. A Lewis structure is not a photograph of a molecule. It does not show three-dimensional geometry; a separate tool, valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, converts the electron count into shapes. It does not show orbitals, the quantum mechanical wave functions that a fuller theory uses; it is deliberately silent about whether a bonding pair lives in a sigma or pi orbital. It treats electrons as neatly localized between two atoms or on one atom, which is often a good approximation and sometimes a poor one; molecules with spread-out, delocalized electrons need several drawings, called resonance structures, to be represented honestly. And for a handful of molecules, most famously oxygen gas with its two unpaired electrons, the simple diagram gets a real property wrong.

Despite those limits, more than a century after their invention, Lewis structures remain the working shorthand of chemistry because they compress an enormous amount of correct prediction into a sketch that takes seconds. Given nothing but a periodic table, a beginner can draw carbon dioxide and correctly conclude that it contains two strong carbon-oxygen double bonds, no lone pairs on carbon, and no charges anywhere, all of which experiment confirms.

Formal charge is the quality-control system attached to this bookkeeping. Because several different Lewis structures can often be drawn for the same formula, all obeying the counting rules, chemists needed a tie-breaker that flags which arrangement of electrons is most plausible. Formal charge assigns each atom a number, positive, negative, or zero, based on comparing the electrons it owns in the drawing with the electrons a free atom of that element carries. Structures whose formal charges are small and sensibly placed are, with known exceptions, closer to reality. Learning to compute and interpret formal charge is what turns Lewis structure drawing from guesswork into a method.

sections.heading: Gilbert N. Lewis and the Shared Electron Pair
sections.body:
The diagrams carry the name of Gilbert Newton Lewis, an American physical chemist born in 1875 who spent most of his career building the chemistry department of the University of California, Berkeley, into one of the world's best. Lewis had been sketching a private model of the atom since around 1902, when, as a young instructor trying to explain valence to students, he drew atoms as cubes with electrons at the corners. The cubic atom looks quaint now, but it encoded a genuinely deep observation: the number eight kept appearing in chemistry. Elements in the main groups of the periodic table combine in ways that suggest their atoms strive for a set of eight outer electrons, an idea the German chemist Richard Abegg had also circled in 1904 with his rule that an element's maximum positive and negative valences tend to differ by eight.

Lewis published the mature theory in 1916 in a paper titled The Atom and the Molecule, in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. Its central proposal was radical for its day: a chemical bond consists of a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. Physicists then pictured atoms as miniature solar systems with fast-orbiting electrons, and the notion of two electrons sitting cooperatively between two nuclei looked almost heretical, since classical electrostatics offers no reason for two negative charges to pair up. Lewis was undeterred; chemistry's facts demanded pairs. He noted that the vast majority of known molecules contain an even number of electrons, that molecules with odd electron counts, like nitric oxide, are rare and unusually reactive, and that pairing plus the drive toward eight explained the composition of thousands of compounds. Quantum mechanics vindicated him in 1927, when Walter Heitler and Fritz London showed that the hydrogen molecule's shared electron pair is stabilized by a purely quantum effect, and Linus Pauling then built modern valence bond theory explicitly on Lewis's electron-pair bond.

The word octet came from a different, larger-than-life figure. Irving Langmuir, an industrial scientist at General Electric and later a Nobel laureate, took up Lewis's theory in 1919, extended it, publicized it in lecture tours, and coined the terms octet rule and covalence. The theory was for a while known as the Lewis-Langmuir theory, to Lewis's considerable irritation, since he felt Langmuir had repackaged his ideas. The community eventually settled the credit where it belonged: the shared pair and the dot diagrams are Lewis's.

Lewis's later career was extraordinary by any measure. In 1923 he published the definition of acids and bases still called Lewis acidity, in which an acid accepts an electron pair and a base donates one, a generalization that unified reactions no proton-based definition could touch. He and his students formalized chemical thermodynamics for working chemists in a landmark 1923 textbook. In 1926 he coined the word photon for the quantum of light. In 1933 he was the first to isolate a pure sample of heavy water. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize dozens of times, more than forty by most counts, and never won, a fact often cited as one of the prize's historic oversights. He died in his Berkeley laboratory in 1946 while working with liquid hydrogen cyanide; the official cause was heart disease. The dot structures he invented for a 1916 argument are now drawn daily by every chemistry student on Earth.

sections.heading: Counting Valence Electrons: The Number You Must Get Right
sections.body:
Every Lewis structure begins with a single integer: the total number of valence electrons available to the molecule or ion. Get this number wrong and everything downstream is wrong, no matter how carefully you place the dots. Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost shell, the ones far enough from the nucleus to be shared with or transferred to other atoms. Core electrons, the filled inner shells, are chemically inert for main-group purposes and are ignored entirely in Lewis bookkeeping.

For main-group elements, the periodic table hands you the count directly, because the American-style group number equals the number of valence electrons. Hydrogen and the alkali metals of group 1 have one. The alkaline earths of group 2 have two. Boron and aluminum in group 13 have three. Carbon and silicon in group 14 have four. Nitrogen and phosphorus in group 15 have five. Oxygen and sulfur in group 16 have six. The halogens, fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine in group 17, have seven. The noble gases of group 18 have eight, except helium with two, which is why they are already content and rarely bond. These numbers are worth memorizing to the point of reflex; they are used constantly.

To count a molecule's total, add up the valence electrons of every atom in the formula. Carbon dioxide, CO2, has 4 from carbon plus 6 from each of two oxygens, for a total of 16. Water, H2O, has 1 plus 1 plus 6, for 8. Methane, CH4, has 4 plus 4 times 1, for 8. Ammonia, NH3, has 5 plus 3, for 8. The count is always for the whole molecule as a pool; at this stage you do not care which atom contributed which electron, and indeed the finished structure may effectively reassign them, which is exactly what formal charge later measures.

Ions require one adjustment that students forget more than any other single step. A negative charge means extra electrons: add one electron per unit of negative charge. A positive charge means missing electrons: subtract one per unit of positive charge. The hydroxide ion, OH minus, has 6 plus 1 plus 1 for the charge, giving 8. The ammonium ion, NH4 plus, has 5 plus 4 minus 1, also 8. Sulfate, SO4 two-minus, has 6 plus 4 times 6 plus 2, for 32. Nitrate, NO3 minus, has 5 plus 18 plus 1, for 24. Phosphate, PO4 three-minus, has 5 plus 24 plus 3, for 32. Always compute the total before drawing a single dot, and write it down; a finished structure must use exactly that many electrons, and checking the tally is the fastest way to catch errors.

Two cautions round out the counting rules. First, the tidy group-number method belongs to the main groups; transition metals hold their d electrons at similar energies to their outer s electrons, their effective valence counts vary from compound to compound, and simple octet-based Lewis structures serve them poorly, which is why introductory courses fence them off. Second, do not confuse valence electrons with valence, the number of bonds an atom typically forms. Oxygen has six valence electrons but a valence of two; carbon has four of each, a coincidence that makes carbon easy and everything else worth double-checking.

sections.heading: The Octet Rule and Hydrogen's Duet
sections.body:
The organizing principle of Lewis structures is the octet rule: main-group atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons until they are surrounded by eight valence electrons. Eight is not numerology. The valence shell of a main-group atom consists of one s orbital and three p orbitals, and each orbital holds at most two electrons, so a filled valence shell holds exactly eight. A filled shell is the electron configuration of a noble gas, the family of elements so stable they were long called inert. When chlorine grabs an electron to become chloride, it achieves the configuration of argon. When sodium sheds one to become a sodium cation, it achieves the configuration of neon. When two chlorine atoms share a pair, each atom counts the shared pair toward its own total and both reach eight. Bonding, in the Lewis picture, is the pursuit of noble-gas electron counts by whatever means are cheapest.

Counting an atom's octet in a drawing follows one convention that must be applied consistently: shared pairs count fully for both partners. An atom's octet tally is all of its lone-pair electrons plus all of the electrons in its bonds. In water, the oxygen has two lone pairs, four electrons, plus two bonds, four more electrons, for eight. Each hydrogen counts its single bond, two electrons. In carbon dioxide drawn with two double bonds, the carbon counts eight electrons from its four shared pairs, and each oxygen counts four from its double bond plus four from its two lone pairs. Note carefully that this octet-counting convention differs from the formal-charge convention introduced later, where shared electrons are split evenly; keeping the two accounting systems straight is half the battle in this topic.

Hydrogen plays by a smaller rule. Its valence shell is the first shell, which contains only a single s orbital and therefore holds a maximum of two electrons, the configuration of helium. Hydrogen therefore follows a duet rule: it forms exactly one bond and never carries lone pairs in ordinary molecules. This has an immediate structural consequence that beginners should internalize early: hydrogen is always a terminal atom, at the end of a bond, never in the middle of a chain, because an atom with one bond cannot connect two neighbors. Helium itself, with its duet already complete, forms essentially no compounds.

The octet rule earns its keep through the second period of the periodic table, the row from lithium to neon, where it is close to inviolable for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine in stable molecules. These four elements are the skeleton of organic chemistry and biochemistry, which is why the rule carries so much weight in practice: the molecules of life obey it almost without exception. Carbon forms four bonds, nitrogen three bonds and one lone pair, oxygen two bonds and two lone pairs, fluorine one bond and three lone pairs; those patterns are the octet rule wearing work clothes.

The rule has honest limits, treated fully in a later section: boron and beryllium often settle for fewer than eight, molecules with odd electron counts cannot give everyone a full octet, and elements from the third period downward, like sulfur and phosphorus, are conventionally drawn with more than eight in species such as sulfuric acid. The octet rule is a powerful default, not a law of nature. Use it as the starting assumption, and let formal charge and known exceptions tell you when to relax it.

sections.heading: How to Draw a Lewis Structure, Step by Step
sections.body:
Drawing Lewis structures is an algorithm, and treating it as one prevents nearly all errors. The procedure below works for the vast majority of main-group molecules and polyatomic ions. Work with a pencil, expect to redraw, and check the electron count at every stage.

The logic of the sequence matters. Counting first fixes your budget. Placing the skeleton second commits the connectivity, which chemical formulas often hint at by writing the central atom first, as in CO2, or grouping atoms as in CH3OH. Filling outer atoms before the center reflects electronegativity: the outer atoms are usually the electron-hungry ones. Converting lone pairs into multiple bonds last is the only step that requires judgment, and formal charge, covered in the following sections, is the tool that guides it.

Worked example one, water. Total electrons: 8. Oxygen is central, two O-H bonds use 4 electrons, the remaining 4 become two lone pairs on oxygen. Every atom is satisfied, hydrogen with duets, oxygen with an octet. Done in ten seconds.

Worked example two, carbon dioxide. Total: 16. Carbon, less electronegative than oxygen, is central. Two single bonds use 4 electrons, and distributing the remaining 12 gives each oxygen three lone pairs. But the carbon now counts only 4 electrons, far short of an octet. Convert one lone pair from each oxygen into a bonding pair: now carbon has two double bonds, an octet, and each oxygen keeps two lone pairs with its octet intact. The count still totals 16. As the formal-charge section will confirm, this symmetric double-bonded structure is the best one.

Worked example three, the nitrate ion, NO3 minus. Total: 5 plus 18 plus 1 equals 24. Nitrogen is central with three N-O single bonds, using 6 and leaving 18, which exactly fill three lone pairs on each oxygen. Nitrogen sits at 6 electrons, so promote one oxygen lone pair to make one N=O double bond. Nitrogen now has its octet. No electrons remain to place, and the whole ion is enclosed in brackets with its minus charge. Three equivalent drawings exist depending on which oxygen takes the double bond, a signature of resonance, discussed later.

Finally, verify. The three-point check, right total, octets and duets satisfied where expected, formal charges computed and sensible, catches virtually every slip a tired or hurried person makes.
steps: Count the total valence electrons for the whole species: add each atom's group-number count, then add one electron for each unit of negative charge or subtract one for each unit of positive charge, and write the total down.
Choose the central atom, which is normally the least electronegative atom in the formula and is never hydrogen or fluorine; carbon is almost always central in organic species.
Draw the skeleton by connecting the central atom to each surrounding atom with a single bond, remembering that every single bond you draw spends two electrons from your total.
Subtract the electrons used by the skeleton from the total to find how many electrons remain to be placed as lone pairs.
Distribute the remaining electrons as lone pairs on the outer atoms first, giving each outer atom, except hydrogen, enough pairs to complete an octet.
Place any electrons still left over as lone pairs on the central atom, even if that gives it more than eight when the element is from period three or below.

If the central atom still lacks an octet, convert one lone pair from an outer atom into an additional bonding pair, making a double bond, and repeat with a second pair, making a triple bond or a second double bond, until the central atom's octet is complete.
Compute the formal charge on every atom, confirm the formal charges sum to the overall charge of the species, and redraw if a different arrangement would give smaller or better-placed charges.

Do the final audit: recount every dot and every line to confirm the structure uses exactly the number of electrons you wrote down in the first step, and enclose ions in square brackets with the charge written outside.

sections.heading: Single, Double, and Triple Bonds: Bond Order in Practice
sections.body:
The number of electron pairs shared between two atoms is called the bond order, and it is one of the most physically meaningful things a Lewis structure displays. A single bond is one shared pair, bond order one. A double bond is two shared pairs, bond order two. A triple bond is three shared pairs, bond order three. No ordinary main-group molecule shares four pairs between two atoms; quadruple bonding is a specialty of certain transition-metal compounds and lies outside Lewis territory.

Bond order translates directly into measurable properties. More shared pairs pull two nuclei closer together and bind them more strongly. The carbon-carbon series makes the trend concrete: a C-C single bond, as in ethane, is about 154 picometers long with a bond energy near 350 kilojoules per mole; a C=C double bond, as in ethylene, shortens to about 134 picometers and strengthens to roughly 610 kilojoules per mole; a C≡C triple bond, as in acetylene, is about 120 picometers and roughly 835 kilojoules per mole. Notice that a double bond is stronger than a single bond but not twice as strong, because the second and third shared pairs bond sideways-on, less efficiently than the first head-on pair. The strongest commonly encountered bond in chemistry is the nitrogen-nitrogen triple bond of N2, at about 945 kilojoules per mole, which is why nitrogen gas, nearly four-fifths of every breath you take, is so famously unreactive that industrial chemistry spends enormous energy in the Haber process just to break it and make fertilizer.

In drawing terms, multiple bonds arise at the step where the central atom's octet comes up short. Consider molecular nitrogen itself. Two nitrogen atoms bring 10 electrons. A single N-N bond spends 2 and leaves 8, which cannot give both atoms octets no matter how they are arranged, since each nitrogen would need three lone pairs. Promote lone pairs into shared pairs twice, and the triple-bonded structure emerges: N≡N with one lone pair on each atom, octets complete, 10 electrons used. The Lewis algorithm forces the triple bond; experiment confirms it.

Bond order also predicts vibration and reactivity. Double bonds are rigid; rotation about a C=C bond is restricted, which is why cis and trans isomers of alkenes are separable compounds with different properties, whereas groups joined by single bonds spin freely at room temperature. Regions of high bond order are also electron-rich targets: the pi electrons of double and triple bonds are the handles by which countless reactions, from bromination to polymerization to enzymatic chemistry, grab a molecule.

When resonance is involved, bond order can be fractional in the averaged, real molecule. In ozone the two oxygen-oxygen links are identical by experiment, each about 128 picometers, intermediate between a typical O-O single bond near 148 and an O=O double bond near 121; the effective bond order is one and a half. In the carbonate ion all three carbon-oxygen bonds measure identically at about 129 picometers, bond order four-thirds, even though any single Lewis drawing shows one double and two singles. The lesson is to read individual drawings as contributing sketches and trust the averaged picture, a point developed in the resonance section. For quick estimation, though, the integer bond orders of a good Lewis structure are usually an excellent first approximation to reality.

sections.heading: Lone Pairs: The Electrons That Do Not Bond
sections.body:
Lone pairs, also called nonbonding pairs, are valence electron pairs that belong entirely to one atom. In a finished Lewis structure they appear as pairs of dots sitting on an atom's symbol, and it is easy for a beginner to treat them as leftover filler, the electrons you park somewhere after the interesting bonding is done. That instinct is exactly backwards. Lone pairs are among the most chemically active features of a molecule, and a large fraction of what molecules do to each other is done with lone pairs.

First, lone pairs shape molecules. The electron pairs around an atom, bonding and nonbonding alike, repel one another and spread out as far as geometry allows. A lone pair, held close by only one nucleus, is fatter and pushier than a bonding pair stretched between two nuclei. The repulsion hierarchy runs lone-pair against lone-pair strongest, then lone-pair against bond, then bond against bond. This is why methane, with four bonds and no lone pairs on carbon, is a perfect tetrahedron with 109.5 degree angles; ammonia, with three bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen, is a squashed pyramid with angles near 107 degrees; and water, with two bonds and two lone pairs on oxygen, is bent to about 104.5 degrees. Same electron count, different shapes, and the lone pairs are the reason. Molecular shape in turn controls polarity: water's bend is why it has a large dipole moment, why it is a superb solvent, and ultimately why oceans dissolve salt and proteins fold.

Second, lone pairs are the currency of acid-base chemistry in its most general form. In the Lewis definition, a base is precisely a lone-pair donor and an acid a lone-pair acceptor. Ammonia is a base because nitrogen's lone pair can grab a proton to form ammonium. Water accepts a proton through an oxygen lone pair to form hydronium. The nitrogen lone pair in amines, the oxygen lone pairs in alcohols and ethers, the sulfur lone pairs in thiols: these are the nucleophiles of organic chemistry, the electron-rich attackers in substitution and addition reactions. When a mechanism's curved arrow starts at a pair of dots, a lone pair is going to work.

Third, lone pairs enable hydrogen bonding, the weak but decisive attraction between a hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom and a lone pair on a neighboring molecule's nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine. Every hydrogen bond in liquid water, in DNA's base pairs, and in protein backbones docks onto a lone pair. Without oxygen's two lone pairs, water would boil far below body temperature and biology as we know it would not exist.

In bookkeeping terms, lone pairs are where most of a molecule's electrons usually reside, and placing them correctly is where most counting mistakes happen. Standard patterns are worth memorizing: in neutral molecules, halogens carry three lone pairs, oxygen two, nitrogen one, and carbon none. Charged atoms shift by one pair per unit of charge in the intuitive direction; an oxygen bearing a negative formal charge, as in hydroxide, carries three lone pairs, while a positively charged nitrogen, as in ammonium, carries none. When a structure's formal charges are being evaluated, the lone-pair count is the first thing to audit, because a misplaced pair changes both the octet tally and the formal charge at once.

sections.heading: Formal Charge: The Formula and What It Means
sections.body:
Formal charge is a bookkeeping number assigned to each atom in a specific Lewis structure. It answers the question: if every bond in this drawing were perfectly, evenly shared, how many electrons would this atom own, and how does that compare with what a free, neutral atom of the element owns? The formula is simple and must become automatic. The formal charge of an atom equals its number of valence electrons as a free atom, minus its number of nonbonding electrons in the drawing, minus half of its bonding electrons. In compact form: FC equals V minus N minus B over two, where V is the group-number valence count, N is the lone-pair electron count, and B is the total count of electrons in bonds touching the atom. An equivalent shortcut many chemists use: formal charge equals valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus the number of bonds, counting a double bond as two bonds and a triple as three.

Work one example slowly. In the hydronium ion, H3O plus, the oxygen has one lone pair and three single bonds. V is 6 for oxygen, N is 2, B is 6, so FC equals 6 minus 2 minus 3, which is plus 1. Each hydrogen has V of 1, N of 0, B of 2, so FC equals 1 minus 0 minus 1, zero. The formal charges sum to plus 1, matching the ion's overall charge, exactly as they must. That sum rule is a built-in error detector: in every correct Lewis structure, the formal charges of all atoms add up to the total charge of the species, zero for a neutral molecule, the ionic charge for an ion. If your charges do not sum correctly, you have miscounted somewhere, full stop.

A more surprising example shows the tool's power. Carbon monoxide, CO, has 10 valence electrons. The only structure that gives both atoms octets is a triple bond with one lone pair on each atom. Compute the charges: carbon has V of 4, N of 2, B of 6, so FC is 4 minus 2 minus 3, minus 1. Oxygen has V of 6, N of 2, B of 6, so FC is 6 minus 2 minus 3, plus 1. The drawing places a negative formal charge on carbon and a positive one on oxygen, despite oxygen being the more electronegative element. This tension is real chemistry: carbon monoxide does have an unusually small dipole moment, with its slightly negative end at carbon, and it binds to metal atoms, including the iron in hemoglobin, through the carbon end, which is precisely why the gas is lethal. Formal charge flagged the strangeness correctly.

Understand clearly what formal charge is not. It is not the actual charge on the atom; real electron distributions are lopsided in proportion to electronegativity, and measured partial charges are usually fractions. Formal charge is the charge under the fiction of perfectly equal sharing. Its cousin, oxidation state, uses the opposite fiction, awarding both bond electrons to the more electronegative partner; the two fictions bracket reality from opposite sides, and a later section contrasts them. Formal charge's job is comparative: it lets you rank rival Lewis structures for the same molecule and identify the atoms where reactivity is likely to concentrate. Negative formal charge marks electron-rich, attack-prone sites; positive formal charge marks electron-poor sites inviting attack. Used that way, within its limits, it is one of the highest-value simple calculations in all of chemistry.

sections.heading: Using Formal Charges to Choose the Best Structure
sections.body:
The counting rules alone often permit several different Lewis structures for one formula, all with correct electron totals and legal octets. Formal charge is the referee. Three ranking principles, applied in order, choose the structure that best represents the real molecule, meaning the one that contributes most to the true, averaged electron distribution.

Principle one: smaller is better. The best structure is the one whose formal charges are closest to zero on every atom, with as few charged atoms as possible. Charge separation costs energy; a drawing that puts plus 1 here and minus 1 there when an uncharged alternative exists is describing a more strained, less probable arrangement of electrons.
