Carbon dioxide is the classic test. The symmetric structure with two double bonds gives carbon and both oxygens formal charges of zero. A legal rival with a triple bond to one oxygen and a single bond to the other gives the triple-bonded oxygen plus 1 and the single-bonded oxygen minus 1. All octets are satisfied in both; the zero-charge version wins and matches experiment, which finds two identical carbon-oxygen bonds of intermediate double-bond length.

Principle two: negative charge belongs on the most electronegative atom. When charges cannot be avoided, and in ions they cannot, since the formal charges must sum to the ionic charge, the better structure parks negative formal charge on the atom best able to stabilize it, the more electronegative element, and positive charge on the less electronegative one. The cyanate ion, OCN minus, illustrates the reasoning. Drawings with different bond patterns place the minus 1 on oxygen or on nitrogen. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so the structure with the negative charge on oxygen, drawn with a carbon-nitrogen triple bond, is the major contributor. The same logic explains why fulminate, CNO minus, the isomer with carbon on the outside, is violently unstable, historically used in detonator caps as mercury fulminate: no arrangement of its bonds can avoid piling awkward formal charges on the wrong atoms, including negative charge on carbon. Formal charge analysis predicts, correctly, that cyanate is the stable arrangement and fulminate the explosive one.

Principle three: avoid like charges on adjacent atoms, and avoid large charges anywhere. A structure putting plus 1 next to plus 1, or any atom at plus 2 or minus 2, is almost always inferior to an alternative that spreads or shrinks the charges. Adjacent like charges repel; big charges signal that the fiction of the drawing has drifted far from a plausible electron distribution.

A worked decision: dinitrogen monoxide, N2O, laughing gas, with 16 electrons and connectivity N-N-O. Three octet-legal structures exist. Structure A, with a nitrogen-nitrogen triple bond and nitrogen-oxygen single bond, gives charges of minus 1, plus 1, zero reading N, N, O... wait, computing carefully: terminal N has plus... Structure A actually yields 0 on the central N never; run the numbers yourself as practice: the two structures that matter place minus 1 on terminal nitrogen with plus 1 on central nitrogen, or minus 1 on oxygen with plus 1 on central nitrogen. Both keep charges small, but the second puts the negative charge on oxygen, the more electronegative atom, so it is the stronger contributor, with the first still significant. Experiment agrees: the real ion is a blend leaning toward the oxygen-negative form. The habit to build is exactly this: enumerate the legal structures, compute every formal charge, apply the three principles, and let the arithmetic, not intuition, make the call.

sections.heading: Formal Charge Versus Oxidation State: Two Different Fictions
sections.body:
Chemistry uses two rival bookkeeping systems for assigning charges to atoms in molecules, and confusing them is a perennial source of lost exam points and muddled thinking. Formal charge and oxidation state start from the same real molecule and the same Lewis structure but apply opposite fictions about who owns the bonding electrons. Formal charge assumes perfect socialism: every shared pair is split exactly down the middle, one electron to each partner, regardless of the elements involved. Oxidation state assumes winner-takes-all: every shared pair is awarded entirely to the more electronegative partner, as if each bond were fully ionic. Neither fiction is true. Real bonds are unequal but not absolute; the actual electron density lies somewhere between the two extremes, which is why the two numbers bracket reality from opposite sides.

Run both systems on the same molecules to feel the difference. In methane, CH4, formal charge gives carbon zero, splitting each C-H pair evenly. Oxidation state notes that carbon is slightly more electronegative than hydrogen, awards carbon both electrons of every bond, and assigns carbon minus 4 with each hydrogen plus 1. In carbon dioxide, formal charges are zero on all three atoms in the best structure, while oxidation states are plus 4 for carbon and minus 2 for each oxygen, since oxygen wins every tug-of-war with carbon. In water, oxygen's formal charge is zero and its oxidation state is minus 2. The two systems agree only when there is nothing to disagree about, as in elemental molecules like N2 or O2, where identical atoms share evenly under either fiction and both numbers are zero.

Each fiction earns its keep in a different job. Oxidation states are the language of redox chemistry, electron-transfer reactions. Because the assignment is systematic, a change in oxidation state is an unambiguous signal that an atom has been oxidized, losing electron ownership, or reduced, gaining it, and balancing complicated redox equations in electrochemistry, metallurgy, and biochemistry leans entirely on tracking these numbers. Combustion of methane to carbon dioxide takes carbon from minus 4 to plus 4, an eight-electron oxidation, and that count is doing real work when you balance the equation or compute a battery's capacity. Formal charge, by contrast, is the tool for structure selection and reactivity mapping within covalent molecules: choosing among resonance structures, locating electron-rich and electron-poor atoms, and predicting where bonds will form and break in mechanisms.

Using the wrong tool produces nonsense. Oxidation states applied to structure selection would tell you the oxygen in water is doubly negative, wildly overstating its charge and predicting ionic behavior water does not have. Formal charge applied to redox would tell you nothing changed when methane burns, since carbon's formal charge is zero in both methane and carbon dioxide, hiding the entire electron transfer. Keep the two systems in separate mental drawers, labeled by purpose.

A memory aid for the mechanics: formal charge is valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus bonds; oxidation state is valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus all bonding electrons the atom wins by electronegativity, with ties split evenly. Both systems obey the same sum rule, totaling the species' overall charge, so both self-check the same way. And both are fictions: measured partial charges, from spectroscopy or quantum calculation, are fractional numbers like plus 0.4, sitting, as always, between the two accountants' extreme reports.

sections.heading: Resonance: When One Drawing Is Not Enough
sections.body:
Some molecules refuse to be captured by a single Lewis structure, and the failure is systematic rather than careless. Ozone, O3, is the standard first example. Its 18 electrons produce a bent chain of three oxygens, and the drawing algorithm forces one oxygen-oxygen double bond and one single bond. But which side gets the double bond? The two choices are mirror images, equally legal, equally charged. Experiment delivers the verdict: both bonds in real ozone are identical, about 128 picometers, squarely between typical single and double bond lengths. The real molecule is not flickering between the two drawings, and it is not half of each in the sense of a mixture. It is one molecule whose four pi-system electrons are spread, delocalized, over all three atoms at once, a situation the localized-pair language of Lewis simply cannot say in one sentence.

The workaround is resonance. Chemists draw all the valid structures, called resonance structures or contributing structures, connect them with double-headed arrows, and declare the real molecule to be the resonance hybrid, the weighted average of the set. The double-headed arrow is a specialized symbol meaning these are partial descriptions of one thing; it must never be confused with equilibrium arrows, which describe genuinely different molecules interconverting over time. A useful analogy: a rhinoceros described by a medieval bestiary as a cross between a dragon and a unicorn is not sometimes a dragon and sometimes a unicorn; it is always a rhinoceros, and the two mythical beasts are just the vocabulary available.

The rules of legal resonance are strict. Only electrons move between structures, never atoms; the nuclear skeleton is fixed. Only pi electrons and lone pairs move, typically a lone pair becoming a bond, a bond becoming a lone pair, or a double bond shifting position. Every structure must have the same total electron count, the same overall charge, and the same number of unpaired electrons. Structures that violate the octet rule for second-period atoms are either discarded or admitted only as minor contributors.

Weighting follows the formal-charge principles already established: structures with smaller charges contribute more, and among charged structures, those with negative charge on electronegative atoms dominate. Equivalent structures, like ozone's two or carbonate's three, contribute equally, and the hybrid's bond orders come out fractional: one and a half for each ozone bond, four-thirds for each carbon-oxygen bond in carbonate, which measures a uniform 129 picometers in every direction, and 1.5 for each carbon-carbon bond in benzene, whose perfectly hexagonal ring, drawn by Kekulé in 1865 as two alternating structures, became the most famous resonance hybrid in science.

Delocalization is not just notation; it is stabilization. Spreading electrons over more atoms lowers their energy, and the difference, called resonance energy or delocalization energy, is measurable. Benzene is roughly 150 kilojoules per mole more stable than a hypothetical ring with three fixed, isolated double bonds, which is why benzene resists the addition reactions that ordinary alkenes undergo eagerly and instead does substitution chemistry that preserves the ring. The carboxylate ion, formed when an organic acid loses its proton, spreads its negative charge over two equivalent oxygens, and that delocalization is a large part of why carboxylic acids are acids at all. As a rule of thumb with wide reach: the more good resonance structures a molecule or ion has, the more stable it is, and species that can delocalize charge form faster and persist longer than those that cannot.

sections.heading: Exceptions to the Octet Rule: Radicals, Incomplete and Expanded Octets
sections.body:
The octet rule is a strong default with three well-mapped classes of exceptions, and knowing them is part of literacy in this subject, because each class contains famous and important molecules.

Class one: odd-electron species, called radicals. A molecule with an odd total of valence electrons cannot pair everything, so at least one atom must carry a lone, unpaired electron, and someone must go without a full octet. Nitric oxide, NO, has 11 valence electrons; the best drawing gives a nitrogen-oxygen double bond, a lone pair on each atom, and the odd electron on nitrogen. Far from being a curiosity, NO is a signaling molecule in human blood vessels, the discovery of which earned the 1998 Nobel Prize in medicine. Nitrogen dioxide, NO2, with 17 electrons, is the brown gas of photochemical smog; its odd electron on nitrogen explains its eagerness to dimerize into colorless N2O4, pairing the two lone electrons into a nitrogen-nitrogen bond. Radicals are typically reactive precisely because that unpaired electron seeks a partner; the chain reactions of combustion, atmospheric ozone destruction, and much of polymer manufacturing run on radical intermediates. A special embarrassment for simple Lewis theory is molecular oxygen, O2: the dot structure with a double bond and full octets pairs all electrons, yet experiment shows oxygen is paramagnetic, drawn into magnetic fields, with two unpaired electrons. Explaining that requires molecular orbital theory; the Lewis picture simply gets O2's electronic structure wrong while still being useful for its bond order.

Class two: incomplete octets, electron-deficient molecules. Beryllium and boron, with only two and three valence electrons respectively, often form compounds where the central atom stops short of eight. Boron trifluoride, BF3, has boron with three single bonds and just six electrons; drawings that fix the deficit with a boron-fluorine double bond put a positive formal charge on fluorine, the most electronegative element of all, which is worse than the incomplete octet. The six-electron boron is real chemistry: BF3 is a powerful Lewis acid, aggressively seeking an electron pair, and it reacts instantly with ammonia's lone pair to form an adduct in which boron finally achieves its octet. Beryllium chloride in the gas phase similarly leaves beryllium with four electrons. The rule of thumb: for boron and beryllium, accept the incomplete octet rather than manufacture bad formal charges.

Class three: expanded octets, also called hypervalence. From the third period downward, elements like phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, and xenon appear in compounds where the conventional drawing gives the central atom more than eight electrons: phosphorus pentachloride, PCl5, with ten; sulfur hexafluoride, SF6, with twelve; xenon tetrafluoride, XeF4, with twelve counting its two lone pairs. Second-period atoms never do this, which is why no NCl5 or OF4 exists. The traditional explanation, that third-period atoms use empty d orbitals to hold the extra electrons, has been largely abandoned by modern quantum chemistry; calculations show the d orbitals are too high in energy to matter much. The current understanding treats these molecules as strongly polarized, with bonding spread across several centers, representable by resonance among structures that keep octets and carry charges, such as drawing sulfate with all single bonds, sulfur at plus 2, and two oxygens at minus 1. For everyday purposes both conventions appear in textbooks: drawing sulfate with two double bonds minimizes formal charges but expands sulfur's octet, while the all-single-bond drawing respects octets but separates charge. Know both, and know which convention your course or context expects.

sections.heading: Polyatomic Ions: Bracket the Whole, Charge the Parts
sections.body:
Polyatomic ions, charged groups of covalently bonded atoms, are where Lewis structures and formal charge earn their keep together, because the ion's overall charge is a hard constraint that the formal charges inside must exactly account for. The notational conventions matter and should be practiced until automatic. The finished structure is enclosed in square brackets with the overall charge written as a superscript outside; inside, individual atoms may be labeled with their formal charges, usually circled in careful work to distinguish them from real ionic charges. The sum of the internal formal charges must equal the external charge, always.

Walk through the most common ions, because these particular species appear everywhere from fertilizer bags to blood chemistry panels. Hydroxide, OH minus, 8 electrons: one O-H bond, three lone pairs on oxygen, formal charge minus 1 on oxygen, zero on hydrogen. Ammonium, NH4 plus, 8 electrons: four N-H bonds, no lone pairs anywhere, formal charge plus 1 on nitrogen. This pair illustrates a rhythm worth internalizing: an oxygen with one bond and three lone pairs is minus 1; a nitrogen with four bonds and no lone pair is plus 1. Those local patterns recur across all of organic and biological chemistry, and fluent readers of structures recognize them at a glance without recomputing, the way fluent readers recognize words without spelling them.

Nitrate, NO3 minus, 24 electrons, was drawn in the step-by-step section: one N=O double bond, two N-O single bonds, nitrogen at plus 1, the two single-bonded oxygens at minus 1 each, the double-bonded oxygen at zero, summing to minus 1. Three equivalent resonance structures average to identical bonds of order four-thirds. Carbonate, CO3 two-minus, 24 electrons, is the same pattern one column over: one double bond, two singles, carbon at zero, two oxygens at minus 1, summing to minus 2, three resonance structures, all bonds equal in the real ion. Sulfate, SO4 two-minus, 32 electrons, admits the two drawing conventions described under expanded octets; in the octet-respecting convention, sulfur carries plus 2 and all four oxygens minus 1 wait, that sums to minus 2 exactly, and in the expanded convention two double bonds reduce the charges. Phosphate, PO4 three-minus, 32 electrons, parallels sulfate with phosphorus at plus 1 in the octet convention and three oxygens at minus 1.

Two practical skills complete the topic. First, recognizing where the reactive site is: the negatively charged atoms of an anion are its nucleophilic, proton-grabbing ends, which is why hydroxide attacks with its oxygen and why the oxygens of carbonate are what bind the calcium ions in limestone and seashells. Second, moving between polyatomic ions and the ionic compounds they build: sodium nitrate is a sodium cation electrostatically paired with the covalent nitrate unit, and a full Lewis description draws the sodium as a bare Na plus beside the bracketed nitrate, with no shared electrons between them. Students who try to draw covalent bonds from sodium to oxygen are mixing bonding regimes; the ion's interior is covalent, its exterior relationships are ionic. Mastering that two-level picture, covalent bookkeeping inside the brackets, ionic bookkeeping outside, is the final piece of fluency this topic asks for.

sections.heading: From Dots to Shapes: What Lewis Structures Feed Into
sections.body:
A Lewis structure is rarely the final destination; it is the input that other predictive tools consume, and seeing the pipeline explains why so much effort goes into getting the dots right. The most immediate consumer is valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, VSEPR, the method that converts an atom's electron-pair count into three-dimensional geometry. The recipe: take the finished Lewis structure, count the electron domains around the central atom, where a domain is a lone pair or a bond of any order, a double or triple bond counting as one domain, and let the domains spread out to maximize their separation. Two domains give a linear arrangement at 180 degrees, three give trigonal planar at 120, four give tetrahedral at 109.5, five give trigonal bipyramidal, six give octahedral. Then name the molecular shape by the positions of atoms only, with lone pairs invisible in the name but very visible in their squeezing of the remaining angles.

The classic series shows the machinery. Carbon dioxide: two double-bond domains on carbon, linear, and the molecule's symmetry cancels its bond polarities, so CO2 has no net dipole, which affects how it absorbs infrared radiation as a greenhouse gas. Water: four domains on oxygen, tetrahedral arrangement, but two are lone pairs, so the molecular shape is bent, the angle compresses to 104.5 degrees, the bond polarities add instead of canceling, and water is strongly polar. Ammonia: four domains, one lone pair, trigonal pyramidal. Methane: four bonding domains, tetrahedral. Boron trifluoride with its incomplete octet: three domains, trigonal planar. Sulfur hexafluoride with its expanded octet: six domains, octahedral. In each case the Lewis structure supplied the domain count, and the geometry followed mechanically.

Geometry plus bond polarity yields molecular polarity, and polarity is destiny for bulk behavior: polar molecules dissolve in water and stick to each other, raising boiling points; nonpolar ones dissolve in oil and slip apart easily. The like-dissolves-like rule of every solubility discussion is Lewis structures cascading through VSEPR into intermolecular forces.

The second great consumer is reaction mechanism. Organic chemistry's curved-arrow formalism is bookkeeping for electron pairs in motion, and its grammar is defined entirely in Lewis terms: arrows begin at a lone pair or a bond, and end where a new bond or lone pair forms; formal charges update according to the same formula this guide has drilled. A student who cannot assign formal charges cannot follow, let alone predict, a mechanism, because the charges are how the page tells you which atom is electron-rich, which is electron-poor, and therefore which end attacks which.

Beyond these lie the quantitative theories. Valence bond theory dresses each Lewis bond in orbital clothing, with hybridization assignments, sp3, sp2, sp, read directly off the VSEPR domain count. Molecular orbital theory abandons localized pairs entirely and, in exchange, fixes the cases Lewis gets wrong, like oxygen's paramagnetism and the one-electron bond of H2 plus. Computational chemistry programs begin from a connectivity that is, in essence, a machine-readable Lewis structure. The humble dot diagram of 1916 thus sits at the base of a tower of increasingly sophisticated models, and the habits it teaches, counting rigorously, respecting charge conservation, and comparing alternative descriptions honestly, are the habits the entire tower is built with.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes, Worked Checks, and How to Self-Audit
sections.body:
Errors in Lewis structures are highly stereotyped; the same half-dozen mistakes account for nearly all wrong answers, which means a short checklist catches them. The most frequent single error is misconstructing the electron total for ions: forgetting to add electrons for negative charges or subtract for positive ones. Ammonium drawn with 9 electrons instead of 8 cannot be completed correctly no matter what follows. Discipline: write the arithmetic explicitly, including the charge adjustment, before drawing anything, and circle the total.

The second classic is exceeding valence limits on small atoms: hydrogen given two bonds or a lone pair, or a second-period atom given five bonds. Nitrogen is the chronic victim; students drawing nitric acid or nitrate routinely give nitrogen five bonds, totaling ten electrons, which no second-period atom can hold since its valence shell has only four orbitals. The correct nitrate drawing keeps nitrogen at four bonds, one double plus two singles, and pays for it with a plus 1 formal charge on nitrogen. When your drawing wants a fifth bond on nitrogen, the molecule is telling you it carries formal charges.

Third, hydrogen placed central, or fluorine given multiple bonds. Hydrogen bonds once, period; it is always terminal. Fluorine in ordinary compounds forms one single bond and never expands; a double bond to fluorine with its positive formal charge on the most electronegative element is essentially always wrong.

Fourth, unbalanced books: structures whose drawn electrons do not match the computed total, or whose formal charges do not sum to the species' charge. Both checks are ten-second audits, and both are absolute; any mismatch means an error exists with certainty. Recount lines and dots, two electrons per line, then compute every atom's formal charge and add them up.

Fifth, resonance mishandled: drawing only one structure for ozone, nitrate, or carbonate and treating its double bond as physically fixed to one position, or connecting resonance structures with equilibrium arrows as if the molecule flipped back and forth. Use the double-headed arrow, and when asked for the real molecule's properties, average: nitrate's bonds are all equal, order four-thirds.

Sixth, misapplying the octet rule's exceptions in both directions: expanding octets on second-period atoms, which is forbidden, or refusing to expand on third-period atoms in conventions that expect it, or manufacturing double bonds to boron to avoid an incomplete octet that is actually the better description.

A complete worked audit, the cyanide ion, CN minus, ties the course together. Count: 4 plus 5 plus 1 equals 10 electrons. Skeleton: one C-N bond, 2 electrons spent, 8 remain. Fill outer octets: this diatomic has no outer-versus-central distinction, so distribute and then promote: a triple bond between carbon and nitrogen, 6 electrons, plus one lone pair on each atom, 4 electrons, totals 10 exactly. Octets: carbon counts 6 bonding plus 2 nonbonding, 8; nitrogen the same, 8. Formal charges: carbon is 4 minus 2 minus 3, minus 1; nitrogen is 5 minus 2 minus 3, zero. Sum: minus 1, matching the ion. Interpretation: the negative charge sits on carbon, the less electronegative atom, an uncomfortable placement the ion cannot avoid, and sure enough cyanide attacks through its carbon end, binding fatally to the iron in the mitochondrial enzyme cytochrome oxidase. Every rule in this guide participated in those five lines, which is the point: the method is a small, closed system of checks, and run in full it is close to error-proof.
